common_name: Marie Ballard Aster (Double Lavender-Blue New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Marie Ballard is a long-cultivated 1950s Ballard-bred selection prized for its fully double, pompom-like blooms.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Marie Ballard is one of the classic Ernest Ballard-bred New York aster cultivars, producing fully double, pompom-shaped, light violet-blue flowers held above mounds of glossy dark green foliage from late summer into autumn, a striking departure from the simple daisy form of the wild species. Its dense double flowers make it a long-lasting cut flower and a reliable source of late-season color for a mixed border. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor and reduce susceptibility to powdery mildew, and stake or pinch back by a third in early summer if a shorter, bushier plant is preferred.

common_name: Patricia Ballard Aster (Semi-Double Clear Pink New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Patricia Ballard is a compact, Ballard-bred New York aster selection with neatly formed semi-double pink flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Patricia Ballard bears bright, clear pink, semi-double flowers with multiple neat rows of petals arranged around a golden center, held above broad, glossy, mid-green foliage from late summer into fall. Bred as part of the historic Ballard family breeding program at Malvern, it forms a comparatively compact, branching clump that spreads gently by short runners rather than sprawling. Divide crowded clumps every two to three years in spring to refresh vigor and reduce powdery mildew pressure, and mulch in autumn to protect the shallow-rooted crown over winter.

common_name: Winston Churchill Aster (Mildew-Resistant Carmine-Red New York Aster)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Winston Churchill is a bushy, branching New York aster selection noted for better-than-average mildew resistance.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade. Winston Churchill produces vivid carmine-red, semi-double flowers with bright golden centers held in a flat, tidy form on a bushy, branching plant from late summer into autumn. It has a long-standing reputation among Michaelmas daisy growers for greater resistance to the powdery mildew that often disfigures New York aster foliage by late summer, and its relatively compact, well-furnished habit suits it to the middle of a mixed border. Divide clumps every two to three years in spring to maintain vigor, and shear back by a third in early summer to encourage bushier, sturdier growth that needs less staking.

common_name: Glutball Joe Pye Weed (Large Reddish-Purple Spotted Joe-Pye Weed)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade; Glutball is a German-selected spotted Joe-Pye weed cultivar noted for its unusually large, rounded flower heads.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Glutball is a selection of spotted Joe-Pye weed grown for its exceptionally large, tightly domed flower heads, which can reach up to 8 inches across and open a deep reddish-purple from mid-August through frost, a richer, more saturated color than many other spotted Joe-Pye weed selections. Like the wild species, it grows tall and imposing when given ample moisture and fertile soil, making it best suited to the back of a border, rain garden, or pond margin where its late-summer color and strong bee and butterfly appeal can be appreciated without crowding smaller neighbors. Divide clumps in spring every few years if a larger planting or renewed vigor is wanted.

common_name: Crown of Rays Goldenrod (Compact Golden Hybrid Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun; Crown of Rays (also sold as 'Strahlenkrone') is a well-behaved clump-forming hybrid goldenrod.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun. Crown of Rays (originally introduced in Germany as 'Strahlenkrone') is a clump-forming hybrid goldenrod that quickly produces dense, horizontal, plume-like sprays of small bright yellow flowers atop stiff, upright stems from late summer into fall. Unlike running native goldenrod species, it stays in a tidy, well-mannered clump that rarely needs division for containment, making it an easy fit for a perennial border or cutting garden. It is a strong draw for bees and butterflies during a late-season nectar dearth and holds up well as a cut flower; divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Golden Baby Goldenrod (Compact Hybrid Cut-Flower Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Golden Baby (also sold as 'Goldkind') is a compact hybrid goldenrod bred for cut-flower production.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Golden Baby (originally released in Germany as 'Goldkind') is a compact clump-forming hybrid goldenrod developed for the European cut-flower trade, producing dense, horizontal plumes of bright golden-yellow flowers on stiff upright stems from late summer into fall. Its shorter stature compared to species goldenrods makes it easier to place in a mixed border without staking, while still delivering the same reliable late-season nectar and pollen source for bees and other pollinators. Keep soil evenly moist through summer to discourage powdery mildew, and divide clumps every few years in spring to maintain a vigorous, floriferous planting.
